metadata.title: LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
metadata.abstract_summary: Replacing DreamCoder's neural search with an LLM-guided synthesizer, and adding an auto-documentation step that names and writes docstrings for learned abstractions from their usage context, lets the system solve more complex tasks and produce libraries that are actually readable by a person, not just functionally reusable by the system itself.

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
As the authors state it:

> While large language models (LLMs) now excel at code generation, a key aspect of software development is the art of refactoring: consolidating code into libraries of reusable and readable programs. In this paper, we introduce LILO, a neurosymbolic framework that iteratively synthesizes, compresses, and documents code to build libraries tailored to particular problem domains. LILO combines LLM-guided program synthesis with recent algorithmic advances in automated refactoring from Stitch: a symbolic compression system that efficiently identifies optimal lambda abstractions across large code corpora. To make these abstractions interpretable, we introduce an auto-documentation (AutoDoc) procedure that infers natural language names and docstrings based on contextual examples of usage. In addition to improving human readability, we find that AutoDoc boosts performance by helping LILO's synthesizer to interpret and deploy learned abstractions. We evaluate LILO on three inductive program synthesis benchmarks for string editing, scene reasoning, and graphics composition. Compared to existing neural and symbolic methods - including the state-of-the-art library learning algorithm DreamCoder - LILO solves more complex tasks and learns richer libraries that are grounded in linguistic knowledge.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Compared directly against DreamCoder and other neural/symbolic library-learning baselines on three inductive program synthesis benchmarks (string editing, scene reasoning, graphics composition), measuring both task-solve rate and, via an AutoDoc ablation, whether documentation itself improves downstream synthesis performance, not only human readability.

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- A direct, controlled comparison against the specific prior system (DreamCoder) it improves on, on the same benchmark family - a stronger evidentiary position than an isolated result.
- Still bounded by the same three benchmark domains as its predecessor.
- The interpretability claim is evaluated by the authors' own inspection and ablation rather than an independent human-subjects readability study.
